newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Ex-police chief appears before S.Africa truth probe.
newsitem.headline: Ex-police chief appears before S.Africa truth probe.

text.p: Apartheid-era police general Krappies Engelbrecht on Thursday became the first person to be forced to appear before South Africa's "truth commission".
Engelbrecht is one of several former security chiefs that the Truth and Reconciliation Commission (TRC) has subpoenaed to testify about what they know of human-rights abuses.
The subpoenas were prompted by the former policemen's reluctance to apply for amnesty to the commission and thereby come clean about their past activities.
The commission has the legal right to subpoena persons it suspects have information that could be useful to it.
Another former police general, Basie Smit, is scheduled to appear before the commission on Friday.
A smiling Engelbrecht refused to answer media questions when he arrived for his day's grilling at the commission's offices.
"I have prepared a report for the commission, I will present that today and hand it in," was all Engelbrecht, said.
The commission said it would not divulge details of the policeman's testimony.

At a news conference on Thursday National Party secretary-general Roelf Meyer denied that party leader and last white president F.W. de Klerk knew of the 1988 bombing of Khotso House, which housed black activists.
Former police commissioner Johan van der Merwe told the commission on Monday that P.W. Botha, de Klerk's predecessor, had given him the bombing order through then police minister Adriaan Vlok.
"I can say that De Klerk was not aware of that (Khotso bombing)," Meyer said.
Former policemen applying for amnesty said this week their operations were regularly reported to the highest government levels of cabinet and the state security council.
But Meyer said his party had made it clear in its submission to the body in August that "we are not going to take responsibility for abuses of power".
He said the NP was preparing another submission over what it had done to prevent abusing power.

The TRC was set up last year to probe human rights violations during 30 years of South Africa's race conflict. It is chaired by Nobel laureate Archbishop Desmond Tutu and has the power to grant amnesty to people who confess to politically motivated crimes.
